title: Lawyer Consultation Fees: Free vs. Paid Consults and What to Ask (2026)
description: Do lawyers charge for consultations? How consult fees work, state bar referral consults from $25, contingency intake, and what to ask before you pay.
summary: Some lawyers offer a free first consultation, especially firms that work on contingency, while others charge a flat fee or bill the meeting at their hourly rate. State bar lawyer referral services often cap the first meeting: for example, 30 minutes for $25 or less through the Illinois State Bar Association, no more than $30 through the Pennsylvania Bar Association and $50 through the North Carolina Bar Association. Before you book, ask what the consult costs, how long it lasts and whether the fee is credited toward your bill if you hire the lawyer.
body:
How lawyers price a first consultation

There is no national standard consultation fee. In practice you will meet four models:

  • Free. Used as a screening meeting. Common at firms paid on contingency, because they only earn a fee if they take the case and recover money.
  • Flat consult fee. A fixed price for a set block of time, often 30 or 60 minutes.
  • Hourly. The meeting is billed at the lawyer's normal rate, sometimes with a minimum.
  • Credited. A paid consult whose fee is deducted from your first invoice if you hire the lawyer.

Example: what an hourly consult costs. Using Clio's 2025 national average rate of $349 an hour[1] purely as an illustration: a 30-minute consult = 0.5 × $349 = $174.50; a 60-minute consult with 30 minutes of document review beforehand = 1.5 × $349 = $523.50. A lawyer's actual rate may be higher or lower.

Reduced-fee consults through state bar referral services

Lawyer referral services run by state bar associations match you with a participating lawyer and, in many states, cap the price of the first meeting. These are some of the fees published by the bars themselves:

First-consultation terms at selected state bar referral services (as published; checked October 2026)
StateServiceFirst consultation
FloridaThe Florida Bar Lawyer Referral Service30 minutes for no more than $25[2]
IllinoisISBA Illinois Lawyer Finder (phone referral)30 minutes for $25 or less[3]
PennsylvaniaPennsylvania Bar Association Lawyer Referral Service30 minutes for not more than $30[4]
DelawareDelaware State Bar Association Online Lawyer Referral Service$35 for an initial 30-minute interview[5]
MaineMaine State Bar Association Lawyer Referral Service$35 administrative fee; first half hour with the lawyer free[6]
North CarolinaNorth Carolina Bar Association Lawyer Referral Service$50 for 30 minutes[7]
AlabamaAlabama State Bar Lawyer Referral Service30 minutes, maximum $50[8]
OregonOregon State Bar Lawyer Referral ServiceUp to 30 minutes, maximum $50[9]
South CarolinaSC Bar Lawyer Referral Service30 minutes, maximum $50[10]
Rhode IslandRhode Island Bar Association Lawyer Referral ServiceFree initial consult of up to half an hour[11]
AlaskaAlaska Bar Association Lawyer Referral ServiceFirst half hour, maximum $125[12]

The reduced fee covers only the first meeting. If you hire the lawyer afterwards, their normal fees apply, so ask for the rate or flat fee in writing at the end of the consult. Fees and coverage change; confirm them when you call. For other states, see our list of state bar referral services or your state guide.

Free vs. paid: what the difference usually buys

A free consult is mainly the lawyer's chance to decide whether to take you on. Expect questions about deadlines, the other party and money at stake, and a general sense of your options. A paid consult is more likely to include advice on your specific facts or a review of documents you bring, because the lawyer is being paid for that time.

Neither is a signal of quality. A free meeting is good value if you need to know whether you have a case worth pursuing. A paid meeting is good value if you need a concrete answer, such as whether to sign a contract or how to respond to a letter, and you may not need a full representation afterward.

Contingency intake calls

In injury and some employment or consumer cases, the first contact is often an intake call or form rather than a meeting. The firm screens liability, damages and insurance before agreeing to meet. If the firm takes the case, ABA Model Rule 1.5(c) calls for a written contingency agreement, signed by you, that states the percentage at each stage and whether case expenses are deducted before or after the fee is calculated[13]. The same rule bars contingency fees for criminal defense and for divorce matters where the fee depends on securing the divorce or on the amount of support or property awarded[13], so expect to pay for consultations in those areas. See contingency fees explained.

Questions to ask before and during the consult

When you book

  • Is the consultation free? If not, what is the fee and how is it paid?
  • How long is it, and what happens if we run over?
  • Will the fee be credited toward my bill if I hire you?
  • Will I meet the lawyer who would handle the case, or an intake specialist?
  • What documents should I bring or send in advance?

At the end of the consult

  • How would you charge for this matter: hourly, flat fee, contingency or a mix?
  • What is your rate, and the rates of anyone else who would work on the file?
  • What is your estimate of the total, and what could make it higher?
  • Is there an advance deposit, and is the unused part refundable?
  • Which costs (filing fees, service, experts) are separate from your fee?
  • Is there a deadline I need to know about right now?

How to get more out of a short consult

  • Write a one-page timeline with dates, names and amounts.
  • Bring the key documents: contracts, letters, court papers, photos, receipts.
  • Put any court papers you were served with on top, and note the date you received them.
  • List your three most important questions so the time goes to them first.
  • Know what outcome you want, including what you would accept to settle.

If you cannot pay for a consultation

If your household income is low, check whether you qualify for legal aid; LSC-funded programs generally serve households at or below 125% of the poverty guidelines, $19,950 for one person in 2026[14]. ABA Free Legal Answers lets qualifying users in participating states post civil legal questions online at no cost, answered by volunteer lawyers[15]. More options are in can I afford a lawyer?

faq.a: Some are. Many contingency-fee firms, for example in personal injury, do not charge for an initial consultation, while other lawyers charge a flat fee or bill the time at their hourly rate. Always ask when you book.

faq.q: How long does a lawyer consultation last?
faq.a: It varies by lawyer. Many state bar referral services set the reduced-fee first consult at 30 minutes, so plan your questions to fit that time and ask what happens if the meeting runs over.

faq.q: Is a consultation fee refundable or credited?
faq.a: Only if the lawyer agrees. Some lawyers credit the consult fee against your first invoice if you hire them; ask before you pay and get the answer in writing or by email.

faq.q: Does a free consultation mean the lawyer will take my case?
faq.a: No. A free consult is usually a screening meeting, and the lawyer may decline the case. If that happens, ask whether they can suggest another lawyer or a referral service.

faq.q: Can I bring someone to the consultation?
faq.a: Ask the lawyer first. Having a third party in the room can affect whether the conversation is treated as confidential, so the lawyer may prefer to speak with you alone for part of the meeting.
